extracted.intended_audience: advanced Latin students, classical/rhetorical scholars, editors and writers interested in Erasmus' principles
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing elegant, effective Latin prose and for editorial practice in preparing classical and biblical texts, based on Erasmus' De Copia and his editorial defenses. Covers style, variety, brevity, usage of Greek, repetition, obscenity, and editorial handling of manuscripts and conjecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech should be fitting, pure, elegant Latin
rubrics_metrics.description: "that speech should be fitting [_apta_], good Latin, elegant and pure [_pura_]".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style is to thought as clothing to the body; words must suit the thought and not spoil it by being mean, unsuited, or of wrong pattern. One must attain purity of Latin before attempting rhetorical abundance; putting on 'copia' before purity is ridiculous. (Analogy of dress and banquet used to illustrate appropriateness.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Copia — richness and variety without verbosity
rubrics_metrics.description: Copia includes the ideas of richness and variety, but must avoid the errors of mere quantity and change; 'Not all fulness contributes to completeness of effect, and not all variation in style helps towards real illustration of the thought.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to condense essentials into few words yet be able to expand without superfluity. Avoid 'feeble and disjointed loquacity' and mere crowded masses of words; ensure every expansion enriches meaning rather than fills space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attain purity before affectation of copia
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not affect 'copia' before you have attained purity of language; otherwise you are as foolish as a beggar dressing rags to seem rich.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid display of variety or ornamentation if your basic language skills are inadequate; practice plainness and accuracy first, then pursue variety and amplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid obscene words except by classical authoritative usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain words are obscene because they represent obscene things; others because they are twisted from harmless meanings. 'What then is the principle of obscenity? -- nothing more nor less than the usage, not of anybody and everybody, but of those whose speech is correct.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from gratuitous obscenity; accept occasional artistic uses (e.g., in colloquies) but rely on the usage of correct speakers/authors to judge propriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek words permitted only for appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Greek words may be used when they are more significant, or shorter, or stronger, or more graceful, 'for no Latin word can equal the grace of a Greek word.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interweave Greek with Latin only when commoditas (appropriateness) invites, especially when writing to learned men; avoid deliberately mixing half Latin and half Greek in adult works — this may be pardoned only in youths training both languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition only when it serves the thought and with variety
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition is disapproved in theory, but may be used 'when the repetition helps the thought and when the weariness of it can be avoided by a certain variety.' Cicero repeats 'things similar, not the same things.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mere affected synonyms and mechanical piling-up of repeated phrases (example: preacher listing many near-identical phrases). Use repetition to illuminate, not to babble.

rubrics_metrics.name: No word is harsh if attested in approved authors
rubrics_metrics.description: 'No word ought to seem to us harsh or obsolete which is to be found in an approved author.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not shudder at words merely because they are not found in Cicero; authoritative classical usage legitimizes otherwise rare or harsh-seeming words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use figures and amplifications only when essential
rubrics_metrics.description: When seeking copia, expand material according to set rules; but the lover of brevity should avoid unnecessary prefaces, feelings, examples, similes, and other figures unless essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present chief arguments compactly; include amplifications, similes, and examples only if they are truly necessary to the point. Do not treat the same subject redundantly in various forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity with aptness, elegance, and simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: "Let him be content to make his point and be very sparing with amplifications... Let each beware, lest through affectation he be carried over into the fault which lies nearest him... For nothing is so conducive to brevity of style as aptness and elegance of words... add simplicity, [and] it will be easy to avoid obscurity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brevity should not mean coldness or obscurity; say the very best thing in the fewest words, choosing apt and elegant diction and simple expression so the matter 'may silently take a certain hold upon the mind.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectation and ostentatious display
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware lest affectation carry you into faults: do not affect copia or display learning for show; avoid mixing incompatible stylistic modes (e.g., prose and verse together) or treating subjects in various forms to show off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer genuine variety that serves thought; avoid rhetorical tricks that exist solely to display wit or learning and thereby undermine dignity and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical rubric for rhetorical exemplars (formulas & practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide formulas and extensive model variations (e.g., variations on 'tuæ literæ me magnopere delectarunt') so that a pupil who practices them intelligently attains mastery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mechanical enumerations and patterned exercises to train readiness and facility in expression — commit substantial parts to memory for practical skill-building, especially for students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial standard: consult ancient manuscripts and use conjecture sparingly but transparently
rubrics_metrics.description: Erasmus: 'The control of ancient manuscripts was not lacking, but these could not preclude the use of conjecture in some places; but these conjectures I so modified in the notes that they could not easily deceive anyone, but could only stimulate in the reader a zeal for investigation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where texts are defective, use conjecture but clearly mark it (e.g., in notes) so as not to deceive; aim to stimulate further investigation and allow future editors to restore points more correctly. Transparency about limits of one’s edition is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial ethic: publish useful (if imperfect) work rather than nothing
rubrics_metrics.description: Defense of publishing imperfect emendations: 'Those who publish nothing avoid all blame, but earn no praise... Whoever says that nothing ought to be published that is not perfect... says that nothing at all should be published.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise contributing usable scholarship to the community even if imperfect; open the way for successors and accept that later scholars may correct and improve; avoid paralysis by perfectionism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-appropriate register and charity toward less learned readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Erasmus edited works 'for Batavians, for monks and theologians, who were for the most part without classic learning; for liberal study had not yet penetrated so far as these.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor editorial and stylistic choices to the intended readership's learning level; provide useful services proportioned to the day and the audience's needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lady Margaret Professorship duties (procedural standard for officeholders)
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader must read _libere_, _sollenniter_, and _aperte_. He must have no fees beyond his salary; must read such works in divinity as the chancellor with the 'college of doctors' should judge necessary; must 'read every accustomed day in each term, and in the long vacation up to the eighth of September, but might cease in Lent, if the chancellor should think fit, in order that during that season he and his auditors might be occupied in preaching.' Election biennial; electors include the chancellor and all doctors, bachelors, and inceptors in divinity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The office was intended to be no sinecure; the holder was expected to devote himself wholly to regular, public, solemn divinity lectures as prescribed and not to receive extra fees beyond the salary.
